segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now we ask you, brothers and sisters, concerning the coming of our Lord Jesus Christ and our being gathered to him,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: not to be quickly shaken from your good sense or alarmed, whether by a spirit or by a spoken word or by a letter supposedly from us, to the effect that the day of the Lord has come.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Let no one deceive you in any way. For that day will not come unless the rebellion comes first and the man of lawlessness is revealed, the son of destruction,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who opposes and exalts himself above every so-called god or object of worship, so that he takes his seat in the temple of God, proclaiming himself to be God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Do you not remember that I used to tell you these things while I was still with you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And now you know what is restraining him, so that he may be revealed in his own time.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For the mystery of lawlessness is already at work; only the one who now restrains will do so until he is out of the way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And then the lawless one will be revealed, whom the Lord Jesus will kill with the breath of his mouth and bring to nothing by the manifestation of his coming.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: The coming of the lawless one is by the working of Satan, with every kind of power and with lying signs and wonders,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: and with every wicked deception for those who are perishing, because they did not welcome the love of the truth so as to be saved.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And for this reason God sends a delusion to work on them, so that they believe the lie,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: so that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but took pleasure in wickedness.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But we ought always to thank God for you, brothers and sisters loved by the Lord, because God chose you as firstfruits for salvation through being made holy by the Spirit and through faith in the truth.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: To this he called you through our good news, so that you may obtain the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So then, brothers and sisters, stand firm and hold on to the traditions you were taught, whether by our spoken word or by our letter.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Now may our Lord Jesus Christ himself, and God our Father, who loved us and by grace gave us eternal encouragement and good hope,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: encourage your hearts and strengthen them in every good deed and word.

notes.note: The Greek word means both arrival and presence, and was the regular term for the state visit of a king or emperor to a city. The same word is used in verse 9 for the arrival of the lawless one, which is presented as a counterfeit of the Lord's own coming.

This most likely means a prophetic utterance claimed to come from the Spirit, and some translations render it ‘by a prophecy’. It is also unclear whether ‘supposedly from us’ applies only to the letter or to all three channels.

Older English versions have ‘is at hand’, meaning near. The Greek perfect tense of this verb normally means ‘is present’ or ‘has arrived’, and most modern translations and commentators take it that way. The claim being corrected was that the day of the Lord was already here, not merely close.

These words are not in the Greek. The sentence begins with ‘unless’ and is never grammatically completed, so translations supply the missing main clause from verse 2. Nearly all agree on what must be supplied.

In the period the word meant revolt or defection, political or religious; in the Greek Old Testament it is used of rebellion against God. ‘Falling away’ suggests a gradual drift, which is weaker than the Greek. Whether a religious defection or a wider revolt against God is in view is debated; a few interpreters have proposed ‘departure’ in a spatial sense, but this has little lexical support.

Many later manuscripts read ‘man of sin’, which is the basis of the older English rendering. The earliest witnesses read ‘lawlessness’, which also fits ‘the mystery of lawlessness’ and ‘the lawless one’ in verses 7 and 8, and most modern editions adopt it.

‘Son of’ is a Semitic idiom for someone who belongs to or is marked out for something, so the phrase means one destined for destruction. ‘Perdition’ is no longer ordinary English. The word is related to the verb behind ‘those who are perishing’ in verse 10.

notes.phrase: takes his seat in the temple of God
notes.traditional: sitteth in the temple of God
notes.note: The language echoes Daniel 11:36, where a king exalts himself above every god, a passage linked to the desecration of the Jerusalem temple by Antiochus IV. Readers would also have remembered the emperor Gaius (Caligula) ordering his statue set up in the temple around AD 40. Whether the Jerusalem temple, a heavenly temple, or the church is meant here is disputed.

notes.traditional: what withholdeth; what is restraining him
notes.note: The Greek has no object (‘him’ is supplied), and the restrainer is a thing in this verse and a person in verse 7. The readers had been told what was meant; later interpreters have not, and proposals include the Roman empire and emperor, God or the Spirit, the preaching of the gospel, and an angel. No view commands a consensus. ‘Now’ may also be read with the restraining: ‘you know what is now restraining him’.

In Jewish and early Christian usage the word means a secret, something hidden for the present and disclosed in due course, not a puzzle. Here it stands in contrast to ‘revealed’ in verses 6 and 8: lawlessness is already operating out of sight before it appears openly.

The Greek word means breath, wind or spirit; here it is breath. The phrase draws on Isaiah 11:4, where the coming king from David's line kills the wicked with the breath of his lips. The point is that no struggle is needed.

The manuscripts are divided between two readings that differ by a single letter: ‘as firstfruits’ and ‘from the beginning’. The SBL text reads ‘firstfruits’, the first portion of a harvest offered to God; many translations follow the other reading. Both are well attested and the choice is uncertain.

The Greek word meant an announcement of good news, such as a victory or a ruler's accession; it was not yet a religious technical term or the name of a kind of book. ‘Gospel’ is the traditional rendering and means the same thing by origin, but many modern translations now use ‘good news’.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed congregations recurs throughout the letters and translators split between 'brothers' and 'brothers and sisters'.
It occurs across the whole New Testament and the choice between 'gospel' and 'good news' should not vary from chapter to chapter.
English 'mystery' suggests a puzzle whereas the Greek means a secret now or soon disclosed; 'mystery' or 'secret' needs to be fixed across Paul, the Gospels and Revelation.
'Sanctification', 'holiness' and 'consecration' are all in use, and the word family (ἅγιος, ἁγιάζω) needs a coordinated rendering.
The noun and its verb παρακαλέω range over 'comfort', 'encourage', 'urge' and 'appeal', and consistent sense-by-sense choices are needed across the letters.
